- If sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.65) in recent days, reduce forecast overshoots, especially after spikes.
- If sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.65), avoid overcorrection downward; allow slight lagged mean reversion.
- When model forecasts show persistent upward momentum after a spike, check for sentiment decay — if sentiment turns negative, reduce forecast slope.
- If true outcome shows early mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days after peak), model should adjust downward slightly, even if sentiment remains bullish.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is volatile or mixed, avoid extreme highs/lows; favor smoother, trend-following adjustments.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes followed by recovery, model should anticipate a “bounce-back” and not overcorrect to the low.
- When sentiment is consistently positive but price fails to rise as forecasted, reduce forecast magnitude by 5–10% to account for sentiment overconfidence.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, model should avoid overfitting to recent highs/lows — use 10–15 day moving average as baseline.
